title: Two kinds of attention
hookLine: focused attention on one object, and open monitoring of whatever arises (Lutz et al.)

cards: A camera has two ways of seeing. Zoom in, and one face fills the frame, sharp to every eyelash, while the background melts away.
Pull back to the wide shot, and the whole street is there at once: the bus, the pigeons, the woman with the umbrella, nothing in particular in focus and everything in view. Neither is the right way.
They're different tools. A group of researchers looking at meditation described it in terms of the same two shots.

teach.b: Antoine Lutz, Heleen Slagter, John Dunne and Richard Davidson wrote a paper on attention in meditation and described two broad styles. The first is focused attention.
You choose one object, the breath at the nostrils, a sound, a word, and rest there.

When the mind wanders, you notice, let go of the distraction, and come back: William James's turn back, done on purpose. The skills it trains are narrow and strong: holding on, catching the drift, returning.
The second is open monitoring. There's no single object. You rest in awareness and notice whatever arises, a sound, an itch, a worry, a memory, without grabbing it or pushing it away.
Then the next thing. The skill here is wide: seeing the whole street without reacting. The authors drew on Buddhist practice for these descriptions.
They say these are broad families, not the only kinds of meditation, and that practices can mix them.
They also describe focused attention as a common way in: steadying the mind first can make open monitoring easier.
Bringing it back is focused attention; catching the idling mind, or wandering on purpose and knowing it, comes closer to open monitoring.
One narrows the beam, one widens it, and a meditator, like a good photographer, learns when to zoom and when to pull back.

how: Some meditation teachers begin students with focused attention on the breath to steady the mind, then introduce open awareness of whatever arises; researchers study the two styles separately because they seem to train different skills.

games.q: what does “two kinds of attention” mean?
o: the attention of beginners, and of experts
resting on one object, or watching whatever arises
paying attention at work, and paying it at home

games.q: two kinds of attention: tap the pairs.

s: open monitoring means focusing hard on one object
that's focused attention. open monitoring has no single object; it notices whatever arises.
the authors say these two styles are the only kinds of meditation
they describe broad families, and say practices can mix them.
focused attention can be a way in to open monitoring
steadying the mind first can make open monitoring easier.

games.q: you're sitting, and a car alarm goes off down the street. you're practicing open monitoring. what do you do?
o: shut it out and return hard to the breath.
notice the sound, let it come and go, and keep watching.
get up and see whose car it is.
games.why: in open monitoring there's no single object to defend. the alarm is simply the next thing that arises, noticed without grabbing.

practice: Spend about a minute in focus: rest on the breath at the nostrils, and when the mind drifts, notice and come back.
Then open: let go of the breath as an anchor and let whatever shows up, a sound, a sensation, a thought, come and go like people crossing a wide street, watching without following any of them.

wordCard.voice: Two kinds of attention. Focused attention rests on one object and returns to it; open monitoring watches whatever arises without grabbing. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: focus, then open. Two shots, two tools, and both are attention. Rest well.

sources.ref: Lutz, A., Slagter, H. A., Dunne, J. D., and Davidson, R. J., Attention regulation and monitoring in meditation, Trends in Cognitive Sciences 12 (2008)
